tasks.title: Add a column
tasks.statement: Add a column active INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 to users. The result is checked against the table contents.
tasks.hint: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN active INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1;
tasks.starter:
-- migration: a new column
ALTER TABLE users

tasks.title: Rename a column
tasks.statement: Rename the column name to full_name (RENAME COLUMN). The result is checked by a query on the new name.
tasks.hint: ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;

tasks.title: Expand and backfill
tasks.statement: Expand the schema: add a column email_norm TEXT and fill it with the email in lower case (NULL stays NULL). The result is checked by a query of id, email_norm.
tasks.hint: First ADD COLUMN, then UPDATE … SET email_norm = lower(email).

tasks.title: Update one batch
tasks.statement: Move the data in batches: set migrated = 1 only for the rows with id from 1 to 4 inclusive (the first batch by key). The result is checked against the table.
tasks.hint: UPDATE … WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 4.

tasks.title: Resume from where it stopped
tasks.statement: The move stopped: the rows up to id 4 are already migrated. Migrate the next batch of 3 rows without touching the ones already done (without hard-coding the bounds, using a subquery on MIN(id) among the unmigrated ones). The result is checked against the table.
tasks.hint: Select ids from the unmigrated rows with ORDER BY id LIMIT 3 and update with IN.
tasks.starter:
-- continue from the last key
UPDATE t

tasks.title: Duplicates before a unique index
tasks.statement: Before creating a unique index on email, delete the duplicate emails, keeping the row with the smallest id (do not touch NULL emails). Then create the index uq_users_email. The result is checked against the table.
tasks.hint: DELETE the rows whose id is not the minimum in the group by email; then CREATE UNIQUE INDEX.
tasks.starter:
-- clean duplicates and create the index
DELETE FROM users

tasks.title: Find duplicates
tasks.statement: Output the emails that occur more than once, and the number of repeats: the columns email, n; ordered by email.
tasks.hint: GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; exclude NULL.

tasks.title: Rebuild a table
tasks.statement: In SQLite a column type is changed by rebuilding the table. Create items_new(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, price INTEGER NOT NULL), move the data with CAST, drop items, and rename items_new to items. The result is checked against items and the column types.
tasks.hint: Create the new one, INSERT … SELECT with CAST, DROP the old one, RENAME the new one.
tasks.starter:
-- the table is rebuilt
CREATE TABLE items_new

tasks.title: Migration version table
tasks.statement: Create a service table schema_migrations(version TEXT PRIMARY KEY, applied_at TEXT NOT NULL) and write two applied versions into it: '001' (applied_at '2026-01-10') and '002' (applied_at '2026-02-01'). The result is checked against the table.
tasks.hint: CREATE TABLE with a primary key on version and an INSERT of two rows.

tasks.title: Which migrations are left to apply
tasks.statement: Output the versions and names of the migrations from available that are not yet in schema_migrations: the columns version, name; ordered by version.
tasks.hint: LEFT JOIN with the filter m.version IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS.

tasks.title: Check after the move
tasks.statement: Compare old_t and new_t by id: output the discrepancies, the columns id, issue, where issue is 'missing' (in old_t, not in new_t), 'extra' (in new_t, not in old_t), or 'diff' (the values v differ); ordered by id.
tasks.hint: Three selects with UNION ALL: left anti-join, right anti-join, and value difference.

tasks.title: Table checksum
tasks.statement: Output a "checksum" of the table: n is the number of rows and s is the sum of id·v (the columns n, s).
tasks.hint: COUNT(*) and SUM(id * v).

tasks.title: Logical backup
tasks.statement: Build a dump: output one row INSERT INTO t VALUES (id, 'name'); for each row (the column stmt, ordered by id). Escape strings with the quote() function; NULL must be output as NULL.
tasks.hint: quote(name) adds the quotes and escapes apostrophes itself; for NULL it gives the word NULL.

tasks.title: Archive before deleting
tasks.statement: Move the orders with created older than 250 (created below 250) into orders_archive and delete them from orders. The result is checked against both tables.
tasks.hint: INSERT … SELECT with the condition, then DELETE with the same condition.

tasks.title: NOT NULL in two steps
tasks.statement: The column city in users still allows NULL. First fill the gaps with the value 'unknown' (UPDATE), then check the result: the result is checked by a query of city by id. (In SQLite, NOT NULL is added after the fact by rebuilding the table; here the first step is enough.)
tasks.hint: UPDATE users SET city = 'unknown' WHERE city IS NULL;
tasks.starter:
-- step 1: fill the gaps
UPDATE users

tasks.title: What to apply
tasks.statement: The available migrations are a list of versions (strings) in arbitrary order, the applied ones are a list of versions. Write pending_migrations(available, applied): a sorted list of the versions that are not yet applied. If the applied ones include a version that is not in available, return the string 'error: unknown <version>' (the smallest such version).
tasks.hint: Set difference; a check for unknown applied versions.

tasks.title: Editing an applied migration
tasks.statement: applied is a dictionary "version → checksum at the time of applying", files is a dictionary "version → current checksum of the file". Write edited_migrations(applied, files): a sorted list of the versions whose checksum changed (the file was edited after being applied), as well as the versions whose file has disappeared.
tasks.hint: Compare files.get(version) with the checksum at apply time.

tasks.title: Migration order by dependencies
tasks.statement: Migrations are a dictionary "name → list of names it depends on". Write order_migrations(deps): the order of applying (dependencies first), choosing alphabetically among the ready ones. If there is a cycle, return None.
tasks.hint: Topological sort: take the ready ones (with no dependencies) alphabetically; if none are ready, there is a cycle.

tasks.title: Linter for dangerous operations
tasks.statement: A migration is a list of SQL strings. Write lint_migration(statements): a sorted list of warnings without repeats: 'drop-column' for ALTER … DROP COLUMN, 'create-index-blocking' for CREATE INDEX without the word CONCURRENTLY, 'update-no-where' for UPDATE without WHERE, 'drop-table' for DROP TABLE. Case does not matter.
tasks.hint: Convert the string to upper case and look for the keywords.

tasks.title: Batch ranges
tasks.statement: You need to process the identifiers from first to last inclusive in batches of size. Write batch_ranges(first, last, size): a list of pairs [start, end] inclusive; the last batch may be shorter; if first > last, an empty list.
tasks.hint: A loop: the end of a batch = min(start + size − 1, last).

tasks.title: Where to continue from
tasks.statement: The batch log is a list of [start, end, status], where status is 'ok' or 'fail'. Write resume_point(log, first): the identifier to continue from, the end of the last successful batch in a row from the start plus 1; if the first batch is not successful or the log is empty, first. The batches go in order without gaps.
tasks.hint: Walk through the log while the status is ok and remember end + 1.

tasks.title: Step compatibility
tasks.statement: A release is a dictionary {'writes': the set of columns the code writes to, 'reads': the set of columns it reads from}. The schema is the set of existing columns. A release is compatible with the schema if all written and read columns exist. Write expand_contract_ok(schema, releases): a list of True/False for each release in order (the keys 'writes' and 'reads' are lists).
tasks.hint: Subset: set(writes) <= schema and set(reads) <= schema.

tasks.title: Point-in-time recovery
tasks.statement: The database is a dictionary "key → value". The backup snapshot was taken at moment 0. The log is a list of records [time, operation, key, value] in increasing time, the operation is 'set' or 'del'. Write restore_to(snapshot, wal, t): the state at moment t (records with time ≤ t are applied). Do not modify the original snapshot.
tasks.hint: Copy the dictionary and apply the log records while time ≤ t.

tasks.title: The moment before the error
tasks.statement: The log is a list of [time, command text]. Write last_good_time(wal, bad): the time of the last record strictly before the first command whose text contains the substring bad (case matters); if there is no bad command, the time of the last log record; if the log is empty, 0; if the bad command is the first, 0.
tasks.hint: Walk through the log, remembering the time of the previous record.

tasks.title: How much data we lose
tasks.statement: The server crashes at moment crash. The log is archived every interval seconds (the archive goes to storage at moments that are multiples of interval: 0, interval, 2·interval, …). Everything written after the last archive is lost. Write data_loss_seconds(crash, interval): how many seconds of data are lost (crash % interval).
tasks.hint: The remainder of the division.

tasks.title: Recovery time
tasks.statement: Recovery = loading the backup (size_gb / read_speed_gbps seconds) + replaying the log (wal_gb / replay_speed_gbps seconds). Write restore_time(size_gb, read_speed_gbps, wal_gb, replay_speed_gbps): seconds, rounded to an integer (everything is positive).
tasks.hint: Two fractions and a sum.

tasks.title: Retention policy
tasks.statement: The backups are a list of day numbers (integers, 0 is today, 1 is yesterday, …). The policy: keep all backups of the last 7 days (days 0–6), and of the older ones keep one per week (a day that is a multiple of 7, and not younger than 7) up to and including 28 days, and delete the rest. Write keep_backups(days): a sorted list of the days that remain.
tasks.hint: Condition: d < 7 or (d ≤ 28 and d is a multiple of 7).

tasks.title: Requests queued on a lock
tasks.statement: A migration takes an exclusive lock on the interval [start, end) (in seconds). Requests arrive at the moments arrivals. A request that arrives inside the interval waits until the end of the lock; if the wait is longer than timeout, the request gets an error. Write blocked_requests(start, end, arrivals, timeout): a pair [number that waited, number that failed by timeout]. The ones that failed also count as having waited.
tasks.hint: For the ones arriving inside the interval, the wait = end − t; compare with timeout.

tasks.title: Verifying a restored backup
tasks.statement: The reference is a dictionary of metrics {'rows': n, 'sum': s}. The restored backup gives the same dictionary, or None if the database did not start. Write restore_ok(expected, restored, seconds, rto): True if restored is not None, both values match, and seconds ≤ rto.
tasks.hint: Three conditions together.
